description: Enacted while Martin was Minister for Education and Science. Its long title provides 'in the interests of the common good for the education of every person in the State, including any person with a disability or who has other special educational needs', and sets a general framework for primary, post-primary, adult and continuing education and for the accountability of schools to students and parents.
significance: The main framework statute for the Irish school system.

law_name: Workplace smoking ban under the Public Health (Tobacco) Act 2002 and the Public Health (Tobacco) (Amendment) Act 2004 (No. 6 of 2004)
description: Martin announced on 30 January 2003 that smoking would be banned in all workplaces, including pubs and restaurants; despite opposition, the ban came into force on 29 March 2004 under the Public Health (Tobacco) Acts.
significance: Ireland was the first country to introduce a nationwide ban on smoking in all workplaces; the European Respiratory Society gave Martin an award for it in September 2004.

law_name: Health service reform programme (2003) and the Health Act 2004 (No. 42 of 2004), establishing the Health Service Executive
description: As Minister for Health and Children Martin launched the overhaul that replaced the regional health boards with a single national body; the Health Act 2004, which established the Health Service Executive (HSE) and dissolved the Eastern Regional Health Authority and the health boards, was enacted after he moved to Enterprise in September 2004.
significance: The HSE has run Ireland's public health services since January 2005.

description: Revoked the Restrictive Practices (Groceries) Order 1987, which had prohibited the sale of groceries below cost, and replaced it with prohibitions of specific anti-competitive practices in the grocery trade. Martin, then Minister for Enterprise, Trade and Employment, moved to abolish the order after the cost of living was scrutinised in RTÉ's 'Rip-Off Republic' series in 2005.
significance: Ended a 19-year ban on below-cost selling of groceries.

law_name: Climate Action and Low Carbon Development (Amendment) Act 2021 (No. 32 of 2021)
description: Government bill of Martin's first cabinet, sponsored by the Minister for the Environment, Climate and Communications (Eamon Ryan). It commits the State to a climate-neutral economy by the end of 2050, introduces five-year carbon budgets and sectoral emissions ceilings, and requires the first two carbon budgets to cut annual emissions in 2030 by 51% compared with 2018.
significance: Put the 2020 programme for government's central climate commitment into law.

description: Enacted under Martin's first government (a bill of Housing Minister Darragh O'Brien), it provides for affordable dwelling purchase arrangements, in which a housing authority holds an equity share in a home sold below market value, for cost-rental dwellings, and for amendments to the social and affordable housing requirements of Part V of the Planning and Development Act 2000.
significance: Statutory basis for affordable-purchase and cost-rental housing.

law_name: Recognition of the State of Palestine (Government decision, 28 May 2024)
description: Announced on 22 May 2024 jointly with Norway and Spain and formally decided by the Government on 28 May 2024, when Martin was Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs; the Government agreed to establish full diplomatic relations and to upgrade the missions in Dublin and Ramallah to embassies. Israel recalled its ambassador for consultations.
significance: A step that Israel's government later cited, with Ireland's intervention in the ICJ genocide case, when it announced the closure of its Dublin embassy in December 2024.

law_name: National housing plan 'Delivering Homes, Building Communities' (November 2025)
description: Successor to Housing for All, launched by Housing Minister James Browne: a target of 303,000 new homes by the end of 2030 (an average of 50,500 a year), 12,000 social homes a year, 90,000 starter homes over five years, and an extra €2.5 billion for the Land Development Agency, whose remit is widened to buying private land. Martin described it as 'the most unprecedented investment in housing ever'.
significance: The government's main response to the housing shortage; CSO completions were 36,284 in 2025.

law_name: Israeli Settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (Prohibition of Importation of Goods) Act 2026 (No. 35 of 2026)
description: Government bill replacing Senator Frances Black's 2018 Occupied Territories Bill. It prohibits the importation of goods originating in certain Israeli settlements, citing the International Court of Justice's advisory opinion of 19 July 2024, and amends the Customs Act 2015. It passed the Seanad in July 2026. Opposition amendments to extend it to services were defeated; the Government cited the Attorney General's advice that a services ban would not be possible.
significance: Described as the first such national ban enacted in the EU; the Government says it continues to seek an EU-wide prohibition.

law_name: Defence (Amendment) Bill 2026 (removal of the 'triple lock'), before the Oireachtas
description: Would remove the requirement for UN Security Council (or General Assembly) authorisation before more than 12 Defence Forces members are deployed overseas with an armed force, leaving approval to the Government and the Dáil. Introduced by Minister for Defence Helen McEntee, it passed second stage in the Dáil by 79 votes to 71 on 21 October 2026 after a debate the Government limited to under four hours; committee stage follows. As of 22 October 2026 it is not law.
significance: The most contested defence reform in decades; Martin says it 'in no way' undermines military neutrality, while the opposition parties call it a betrayal and demand a referendum.
